vignette: When Rohan, a 58-year-old product manager at a Silicon Valley startup, was still a teenager, he was kidnapped by an insurgent group during a pilgrimage in the mountains of his native Punjab. In the cramped, dimly lit cell that became his first ordeal, he endured a series of beatings and electric shocks while being forced to watch men speaking in a language he could not comprehend. The noise of their harsh chatter, the abrupt clang of steel on stone, and the relentless pounding of a nearby mortar gave him a terror that he could never shake. He was left with a scar that burned like a small, relentless electric current, a scar that would later flare whenever he heard any dissonant chatter or the distant wail of a siren. After his release, Rohan could not shake the feeling that the world itself had turned hostile. He came to believe that people could not be trusted, that something intrinsic about him had doomed him to this fate, and that nothing good could ever happen to him again. Those negative appraisals seeded a cautiousness that spilled into his daily life. He avoided stressful situations at work, declining to take on projects with tight deadlines or to present to large audiences. He also began to check his pulse, his breathing, and the temperature of his skin as if he were on a battlefield, constantly monitoring his body for signs of impending danger. In this way, his distorted beliefs about the world directly fueled the maladaptive strategies he adopted to survive. The same negative appraisals also heightened his sense of threat. Rohan could not relax, even in his own apartment, feeling that any moment might bring a new attack. He woke nightly, half-awake, scanning the darkness for sounds that might signal danger. The mere thought that a stranger might touch him made his heart race; a light touch from a co-worker's hand would set him on high alert. He had come to believe that the world was perpetually on the verge of violence, a threat that could not be contained or avoided. When this threat perception was coupled with the chaotic sounds that often filled the street outside his building-sirens, distant gunfire, or the chatter of hurried crowds-Rohan's maladaptive strategies intensified. He began to steer clear of conference rooms, opting instead for quiet corners of the office where he could monitor the environment. He would leave early or stay late to avoid the clamor of the main hallway. These movements reinforced his sense that he was being hunted, making his threat perception more urgent. The same threat also acted as a trigger for his re-experienced symptoms. The incomprehensible chatter that he once heard in the cell now echoed in the language of a foreign tech partner he met at a networking event. The sirens that once announced a battle now sounded like the alarm of an emergency drill during a client call. Even a sudden light breeze could trigger a dizzy spell, as if the wind were a shuddering rope pulling him back into the cell. Each of these triggers amplified his threat, creating a vicious cycle that tightened with every passing day. In the end, Rohan's maladaptive strategies, borne out of his negative appraisals and threatened by everyday sounds, fed back into his worldview. Avoiding stressors and constantly checking his body left him feeling chronically exhausted and helpless, evidence that his mistrust of people was justified. Each time he avoided a meeting or left early, he reinforced the belief that the world was hostile and that nothing good could come from it. As his daily life became more isolated, his fear of touching, his nighttime vigilance, and his dizziness during ordinary sounds compounded, leaving him on the verge of burnout and social withdrawal. It was this cumulative erosion of his functioning and the relentless terror that finally prompted Rohan to seek help, hoping that a clinician might untangle the loop that bound his past to his present.
